claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in tungsten-based plasma-facing materials is governed by uniformly distributed nanoscale carbide precipitates.
High-temperature toughness in tungsten-based plasma-facing materials is governed by uniformly distributed nanoscale carbide precipitates.
Nanoscale carbide precipitates facilitate dislocation climb by acting as vacancy sinks.
Conventional processing of tungsten alloys generally produces a coarse microstructure.
Conventional processing of tungsten alloys generally produces a low density or inhomogeneous distribution of carbide precipitates.
Thermomechanical processing or powder-metallurgical routes can introduce a fine, uniform dispersion of nanoscale carbide precipitates into tungsten alloys.
Temperatures of 1300–1600 °C are representative of fusion plasma-facing component operating conditions.
Carbide precipitates acting as vacancy sinks promote dislocation climb in tungsten.
Promoted dislocation climb enhances the ability of tungsten alloys to accommodate plastic strain.
Promoted dislocation climb delays catastrophic failure of tungsten alloys at elevated temperature.
A uniform precipitate distribution increases the frequency of effective dislocation-obstacle interactions.
More frequent dislocation-precipitate interactions enable plastic deformation at elevated temperatures.
An engineered tungsten alloy containing finely dispersed carbide precipitates should have greater strain to failure than the conventional baseline under identical high-temperature conditions.
An engineered tungsten alloy containing finely dispersed carbide precipitates should absorb more fracture energy than the conventional baseline under identical high-temperature conditions.
A conventionally processed tungsten-alloy baseline without controlled nanoprecipitate dispersion is expected to have lower high-temperature plasticity.
A conventionally processed tungsten-alloy baseline without controlled nanoprecipitate dispersion is expected to have lower high-temperature toughness.
The proposed effect should hold when dislocation climb is the dominant deformation mechanism.
The proposed effect may not hold at lower temperatures or when other deformation mechanisms predominate.
